The holy grail of investing is knowing how to balance.

When you can take equally good things where your expectation of return is equal, but because they are uncorrelated and move differently, they balance each other. That is how you can reduce your risk without reducing your returns.

You have to understand that the market is a zero-sum game. The consensus is already reflected in the price, and trying to beat it is a difficult game. In fact, it is more difficult to compete and be successful in the markets than it is to compete in the Olympics. We must be humble about that.

But achieving that balance so you can get a good return without losing a lot of money is everything. Most of my own money is invested in exactly that.

My best explanation of the “software factory” is to literally think about engineering output as a factory.

Before AI, software was mostly craftsmanship. The craftsmen were software engineers, and we spent decades optimizing everything around them: PMs writing specs so engineers worked on the right thing, better tooling, CI/CD, testing, infra, etc. But ultimately the throughput of the factory was still constrained by how much software humans could physically write.

Then the first wave of AI made the craftsmen much faster. Autocomplete, Cursor-style coding, pair programming with AI.

Now agents can increasingly take a feature end to end: understand the spec, inspect the codebase, write the code, test it, fix it, ship it. So for roughly the same human input, the output of the software factory starts going up dramatically.

And I think the end state people are chasing is a mostly autonomous software factory. Engineers write a spec / markdown file, define the tests and constraints, and become much more like verification engineers, while swarms of agents run 24/7 looking at telemetry, customer bugs, regressions, feature requests, then designing, coding, testing and shipping software.

But for that to actually work, the rest of the factory has to be insanely good too: CI/CD, tests, fast deployments, observability, security, rollback, evals, all of it.

It’s basically going from Ferrari building cars with incredible craftsmen doing a huge amount by hand, to the most advanced Tesla-style factory where more and more of the production line is automated.

And the big assumption behind all of this is that your product will eventually be as good as your software factory. If your factory is better, your agents can iterate faster, learn faster, ship more, and ultimately just build a better product.

Yesterday I got a bit roasted on X because I said my agent checks me in for my flights, so let me double down: it also helps me book basically every plane ticket.

I just landed in India and they asked for one of those crazy health/immigration forms with passport info, where you’re staying, flight details, etc. I sent it to my agent, it filled everything out, great job, I went back to reading my book.

A bunch of people replied: “I’m a competent adult, I know how to do this, I don’t need AI.”

Which is totally fair. Do whatever works for you! 

I also know how to wash dishes and I love my dishwasher. I know how to write a letter, put it in an envelope and go to the post office, and yet I prefer email. I know how to do mental arithmetic and I still use a calculator.

The point of technology is very rarely that humans are incapable of doing the thing. It’s that our time and attention are better spent somewhere else.

Instead of spending 20 minutes fighting with a PDF, finding my passport number, hotel address and flight information in five different places, I can read my book. Instead of manually replying to three emails just to send my landlord some insurance information, an agent can handle it and I get another 20 minutes with my 18-month-old daughter, Josephine.

I think people underestimate AI agents for two reasons.

First, capitalism has this amazing tendency to take things that were once reserved for rich people and, through technology and scale, give them to everyone. Rich people have had executive assistants forever. Someone books their flights and restaurants, coordinates meetings, answers routine communications, fills out paperwork, reminds them what they forgot. AI is going to give some version of that to billions of people.

Second, a huge amount of economic progress is simply removing friction. Coase would call a lot of this transaction costs. One form takes 15 minutes, one email takes 3 minutes, one reservation takes 10 minutes. None of these things individually feels revolutionary, but remove thousands of them over a lifetime and it compounds into something enormous.

So yes, I am perfectly capable of checking myself into a flight but now I just don’t see why I should.
